passages.source_text: καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ὅταν εἰς ἕκαστον ὧν προέτεινα διαλεχθεὶς σοι τῆς κακίας τὸν αἴτ[ιον] δείξω, τότε σοι καὶ πρὸς ἃ εἴρηκας [ἀ]ποκρινοῦμαι, καὶ ὃν φῂς θεὸν ἄμεμ[πτον] ὑπὸ μέμψιν εἶναι ἀποδείξω. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἐπειδὴ ἀφ’ ὧν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς φθέγγει συννοῶ σε μηδὲν ἕτερον σπουδάζοντα ἢ ὡς κακίας ἡγεμόνα τὸν θεὸν ὑποβάλλειν μέμψει, προῄρημαι πάσαις αἷς βούλει ὁδοῖς συνοδεύων δεῖξαι θεὸν πάσης μέμψεως ἐκτὸς ὄντα. καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Ταῦτα ὡς ἀγαπῶν θεὸν ὃν νενόμικας λέγεις, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἀληθεύεις. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Σὺ δὲ ὡς κακὸς μισῶν θεὸν ὃν ἠγνόησας, βλασφήμους ἀφίης φωνάς. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Μνημόνευε ὅτι με κακίας ἡγεμόνι παρείκασας. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ὁμολογῶ ἐψευσάμην παρεικάσας σε τῷ πονηρῷ· ἠναγκάσθην γὰρ ἐπὶ τῷ μὴ εὑρεῖν τὸν σὸν ἴσον ἢ καὶ χείρονά. τούτου ἕνεκα τῷ πονηρῷ σε παρείκασα· [σὺ γ]ὰρ καὶ τοῦ τῆς κακίας ἡγεμόνος [πολ]λῷ πονηρότερος τυγχάνεις· τὸν γὰρ [πο]νηρὸν οὐδεὶς κατειπόντα θεοῦ δεῖξαι δύναται, σὲ δὲ τολμηρῶς καταλέγοντα οἱ πάντες παρόντες ἱστοροῦμεν. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ὁ ἀλήθειαν ζητῶν οὐδὲν οὐδενὶ ὀφείλει παρὰ τὸ ὂν χαρίζεσθαι· ἐπεὶ τί καὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν ζητεῖ; τί δέ; καὶ ἐγὼ οὐ δύναμαι, παρεὶς ἀκριβοῦν τὰ πράγματα, εἰς ἐγκώμιον οὗ μὴ ἐπίσταμαι θεοῦ τὸν πάντα μου δαπανᾶν χρόνον;

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Οὔτε τοσοῦτον εἶ μακάριος αὐτὸν ὑμνεῖν, οὔτε μὴν τὸ ἀγαθὸν τοῦτο ποιῆσαι δύνασαι· αὐτοῦ γὰρ πλήρης ἂν ᾖς. οὕτω γὰρ ὁ ἀψευδὴς ἡμῶν εἶπε διδάσκαλος „ἐκ περισσεύματος καρδίας στόμα λαλεῖ“. ὅθεν σὺ περισσευόμενος προαιρέσει κακῇ ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ καταλέγεις τοῦ μόνου ἀγαθοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ μήπω κατ’ ἀξίαν πάσχων ὧν ἐτόλμησας λέγειν. εἰ [κρί]σιν οἴει μὴ ἔσεσθαι, τάχα δὴ μηδὲ εἶναι θεὸν νομίζεις. ὅθεν τῆς τοσαύτ[ης] αὐτοῦ μακροθυμίας οὐκ ἀντιλαμβανόμενος ἐπὶ πλεῖον πρὸς ἀπόνοιαν αὐτὸν ἐκτείνεις. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Μὴ ἔλπιζε φόβῳ δυσωπήσειν με μὴ ζητεῖν σοι τῶν παραδειγμάτων τὰ ἀληθῆ· ἐγὼ γὰρ τοσοῦτον ἀληθείας ὀρέγομαι ὡς αὐτῆς ἕνεκα μὴ ὀκνῆσαι καὶ τὸ κινδυνεύειν ἀναδέχεσθαι. πλὴν πρὸς τὰ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς σοι ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ προταθέντα, εἴγε εἰπεῖν ἔχεις, ἤδη λέγε.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἐπειδὴ τολμᾶν ἡμᾶς ἀναγκάζεις τὰς τοῦ θεοῦ τέχνας ἀκριβῶς ἐφευρόντας λέγειν, καὶ ταῦτα ἀνθρώπους τοὺς μηδὲ τῶν ὁμοίων τὰς τέχνας ἀκριβῶσαι δυναμένους, διὰ γοῦν τοὺς παρεστῶτας ἀντὶ τῆς εὐσεβεστάτης σιγῆς περὶ ὧν θέλεις διαλεχθήσομαι. συνο[μο]λογῶ σοι εἶναί τινα κακίας ἡγεμόνα, [οὗ] τὴν γένεσιν ἡ γραφὴ οὔτε ἀληθὲς [οὔ]τε ψευδὲς εἰπεῖν ἐτόλμησεν. πλὴν συνδιαπορήσωμεν πολλαχῶς τὸ πῶς γέγονεν (εἴπερ γέγονεν) καὶ τῶν δοκούντων τὸ εὐφημότερον ἑλώμεθα, ἐπεὶ ἐκ τῶν εἰκότων λαμβάνεται τοῦτο βεβαίως, ὃ μὲν ὅτι θεῷ τὸ εὐφημότερον δοῦναι πρέπει, ταύτῃ μᾶλλον πασῶν ὑπονοιῶν καθαρθεισῶν καὶ ἄλλης ἱκανῆς καὶ ἀκινδυνοτέρας παρακειμένης ὑποψίας. πλὴν ἤδη σοι πρὸ τῆς ζητήσεως ὑπισχνοῦμαι ὅτι πᾶσα ὁδὸς ζητήσεως ἄμεμπτον αὐτὸν μόνον δύναται δεῖξαι τὸν θεόν.

πλὴν (ὡς ἔφης) ὁ πονηρὸς εἰ γενητός ἐστιν, ἢ ὡς ζῷον γεγένηται ἢ οὐσιωδῶς ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ προβέβληται ἢ ἔξω κέκραται ἢ τῇ κράσει συμβέβηκεν αὐτοῦ ἡ προαίρεσις ἢ ἄνευ κράσεως καὶ θεοῦ βουλῆς συνέβη γενέσθαι· ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων ἢ ὑπὸ θεοῦ ἐκ [τοῦ] μηδαμῇ μηδαμῶς γέγονεν ἢ ἐκτ[ὸς] ἦν θεοῦ ἢ ὕλη ἄψυχος οὖσα ἢ ἔμψυχος ὅθεν γέγονεν ἢ ἑαυτὸν δημιουργήσας ἢ ὑπὸ θεοῦ γεγονὼς ἢ τῶν πρὸς τὶ ἐστὶν ἢ ἀεὶ ἦν. εἰπεῖν γὰρ αὐτὸν μὴ εἶναι οὐ δυνάμεθα· συνωμολογήσαμεν γὰρ αὐτὸν ὑπάρχειν. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Καλῶς πάσας αὐτοῦ τὰς ὁδοὺς διεῖλες, τὸ κεφάλαιον αὐτοῦ· λοιπὸν ἐμόν ἐστι τὴν διαίρεσιν ἀνακρίναντα δεῖξαί σοι τὸν δημιουργὸν ὑπὸ μέμψιν ὄντα· σοῦ δὲ ἔργον ἀποδεῖξαι αὐτὸν (ὡς ὑπέσχησαι) πάσης μέμψεως ἐκτὸς ὄντα· θαυμάζω δὲ εἰ δυνήσῃ. πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ ὁ πονηρός, εἰ ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ζῷον γεγένηται, ἀκολούθως τῆς αὐτῆς τοῦ προβάλλοντος κακίας τυγχάνει. καὶ [ὁ Πέτ]ρος Οὐ πάντως· ὁρῶμεν γὰρ πολ[λοὺ]ς τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀγαθοὺς ὄντας καὶ [κα]κοὺς γεννήσαντας, ἄλλους δὲ [κα]κοὺς ὑπάρχοντας καὶ ἀγαθοὺς ἐσχηκότας, ἑτέρους δὲ κακοὺς ὄντας καὶ ἀγαθοὺς προβάλλοντας, ἄλλους δὲ ἀγαθοὺς ὑπάρχοντας καὶ κακούς τε καὶ ἀγαθοὺς τεκνώσαντας. αὐτίκα γοῦν ὁ πρῶτος δημιουργηθεὶς ἄνθρωπος ἐγέννησεν τὸν ἄδικον Κάϊν καὶ τὸν δίκαιον Ἄβελ. πρὸς ταῦτα ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Ἀνοήτως ποιεῖς περὶ θεοῦ διαλεγόμενος ἀνθρωπίνοις χρώμενος παραδείγμασιν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Σὺ οὖν ἡμῖν λέγε περὶ θεοῦ, ἀνθρωπίνοις μὴ χρώμενος παραδείγμασιν, μετὰ τοῦ μέντοι νοηθῆναι δύνασθαι τὰ λεγόμενα· ἀλλ’ οὐ δυνήσῃ.

αὐτίκα γοῦν τί τὴν ἀρχὴν ἔλεγες; εἰ ἐκ θεοῦ ὁ πονηρὸς γεγένηται, τῆς αὐτῆς αὐτῷ ὢν οὐσίας, καὶ πονηρός ἐστιν. ἐμοῦ δὲ δείξαντος ἐ[ξ οὗ]περ αὐτὸς ἔδωκας παραδείγματο[ς] ὅτι ἐξ ἀγαθῶν κακοὶ γίνονται καὶ ἐ[κ] κακῶν ἀγαθοί, οὐ παρεδέξω, ἀνθρώ- .πινον φήσας εἶναι τὸ παράδειγμα. ὅθεν καὶ νῦν ἐγὼ οὐδὲ τὸ γεγεννῆσθαι θεὸν παραδέχομαι, ὅτι τὸ γεννᾶν ἀνθρώπων ἐστίν, οὐ θεοῦ. ἀλλ’ οὔτε ἀγαθὸς ἢ κακὸς ἢ δίκαιος ἢ ἄδικος εἶναι δύναται ὁ θεός, οὔτε μὴν φρόνιμος ἢ ζῷον ἢ ὅσα ἄλλα ἀνθρώποις προσεῖναι δύναται· ἀνθρώπων γὰρ τὰ τοιαῦτα. καὶ εἰ μὴ χρὴ ζητοῦντας περὶ θεοῦ διδόναι αὐτῷ τὰ ἀνθρώποις προσόντα καλά, οὐδέν ἐστιν τοῦ λοιποῦ νοεῖν ἢ λέγειν ἢ τοῦτο μόνον ζητεῖν, τὸ τῆς προαιρέσεως αὐτοῦ, ἣν αὐτὸς συνεχώρησεν ἡμῖν νοεῖν, ὅπως κρινόμενοι ἀναπολόγητοι ὦμεν περὶ ὧν γνόντες οὐκ ἐφυλάξαμεν.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

And Simon said, “When I have discussed with you each of the points I proposed and shown you who is responsible for evil, then I will also answer what you have said and demonstrate that the God whom you call blameless is liable to blame.”

And Peter said, “Since, from what you have been saying from the beginning, I perceive that you are intent on nothing other than subjecting God to blame as the leader of evil, I have resolved to accompany you along every path you wish and show that God is beyond all blame.”

And Simon said, “You say these things as one who loves the one you have taken to be God, but you are not speaking the truth.”

And Peter said, “But you, as an evil man who hates the God you have failed to know, let loose blasphemous words.”

And Simon said, “Remember that you compared me to a leader of evil.”

And Peter said, “I confess that I lied when I compared you to the evil one, for I was compelled to do so because I could not find anyone equal to you or even worse than you. That is why I compared you to the evil one, for you prove to be much more wicked than even the leader of evil. No one can show that the evil one has spoken against God, but all of us who are present can attest that you boldly denounce him.”

And Simon said, “One who seeks the truth owes it to no one to concede anything contrary to what is. Otherwise, why does he seek at all? What then? Could I not likewise, setting aside an exact investigation of the facts, spend all my time praising a God whom I do not know?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς κακίας τὸν αἴτ[ιον]
lexical_decisions.chosen: who is responsible for evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine substantive αἴτιος can identify the responsible agent or cause. The personal wording suits the ensuing inquiry into the leader of evil.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς κακίας ἡγεμόνα τὸν θεὸν ὑποβάλλειν μέμψει
lexical_decisions.chosen: subjecting God to blame as the leader of evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑποβάλλειν μέμψει depicts placing or exposing someone under censure, while ὡς κακίας ἡγεμόνα states the alleged basis for that censure.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: θεὸν ὃν νενόμικας
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one you have taken to be God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect of νομίζω presents Peter as having regarded or supposed this one to be God. “The God in whom you have believed” is possible but less directly reflects the verb’s evaluative sense.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν γὰρ [πο]νηρὸν οὐδεὶς κατειπόντα θεοῦ δεῖξαι δύναται
lexical_decisions.chosen: No one can show that the evil one has spoken against God
lexical_decisions.rationale: καταλέγω here means speak against, denounce, or malign. The rendering does not import the broader claim that the evil one never otherwise opposes God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲν οὐδενὶ ὀφείλει παρὰ τὸ ὂν χαρίζεσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: owes it to no one to concede anything contrary to what is
lexical_decisions.rationale: χαρίζεσθαι can mean grant a favor or make a concession, and παρὰ τὸ ὄν contrasts such favor with reality as it is.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἐγὼ οὐ δύναμαι, παρεὶς ἀκριβοῦν τὰ πράγματα, εἰς ἐγκώμιον οὗ μὴ ἐπίσταμαι θεοῦ τὸν πάντα μου δαπανᾶν χρόνον;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Could I not likewise, setting aside an exact investigation of the facts, spend all my time praising a God whom I do not know?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed question is taken as a sarcastic question about what Simon could do instead of investigating. οὗ μὴ ἐπίσταμαι θεοῦ is understood as an attracted relative construction referring to the unknown God.

passages.text:
And Peter said, “You are not blessed enough to praise him, nor indeed are you able to do this good thing, for then you would be full of him. For this is what our teacher, who does not lie, said: ‘A mouth speaks from the heart’s abundance.’ Therefore you, overflowing with an evil purpose because of ignorance, speak against the only good God, without yet suffering what your daring words deserve. If you suppose there will be no judgment, perhaps you actually think there is no God. Therefore, because you fail to recognize such great patience on his part, you drive him still further toward desperate action.”

And Simon said, “Do not hope to cow me with fear so that I refrain from seeking from you what is true in the examples. I long so greatly for truth that, for its sake, I would not hesitate to undertake even the risk. But concerning the points I proposed to you at the beginning—if indeed you have anything to say—speak now.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Οὔτε τοσοῦτον εἶ μακάριος αὐτὸν ὑμνεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: You are not blessed enough to praise him
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοσοῦτον with the infinitive expresses the degree required for praising God, not merely the quantity of praise.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκ περισσεύματος καρδίας στόμα λαλεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: A mouth speaks from the heart’s abundance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering follows the wording supplied here rather than harmonizing it with a familiar canonical form; the Greek has neither a definite article before “mouth” nor an added possessive.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν σὺ περισσευόμενος προαιρέσει κακῇ ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ καταλέγεις τοῦ μόνου ἀγαθοῦ θεοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: Therefore you, overflowing with an evil purpose because of ignorance, speak against the only good God
lexical_decisions.rationale: προαίρεσις denotes a chosen disposition, purpose, or moral intention. The causal expression ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ is attached to that evil purpose; it could instead qualify the act of speaking against God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν τῆς τοσαύτ[ης] αὐτοῦ μακροθυμίας οὐκ ἀντιλαμβανόμενος ἐπὶ πλεῖον πρὸς ἀπόνοιαν αὐτὸν ἐκτείνεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: Therefore, because you fail to recognize such great patience on his part, you drive him still further toward desperate action
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine αὐτόν most directly refers to God, making him the object of ἐκτείνεις. ἀπόνοια can denote desperation, recklessness, or drastic resolve. An alternative contextual interpretation is “you extend yourself still further into recklessness,” but that requires taking αὐτόν reflexively or loosely.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φόβῳ δυσωπήσειν με μὴ ζητεῖν σοι τῶν παραδειγμάτων τὰ ἀληθῆ
lexical_decisions.chosen: cow me with fear so that I refrain from seeking from you what is true in the examples
lexical_decisions.rationale: δυσωπέω can mean shame, overawe, or intimidate. The infinitive with μή states the result Simon rejects, while σοι marks Peter as the person from whom the truth is sought.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἴγε εἰπεῖν ἔχεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: if indeed you have anything to say
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom concerns having something available to say, not merely possessing the physical ability to speak.

passages.text: And Peter said, “Since you force us to dare to speak as people who have accurately discovered God’s methods—and this though we are humans unable to ascertain precisely even the methods of those like ourselves—then, at least for the sake of those standing by, I will discuss what you wish instead of maintaining the most reverent silence. I agree with you that there is a certain leader of evil, about whose origin Scripture did not dare to say either something true or something false. Nevertheless, let us explore together, from many angles, how he came to be—if indeed he came to be—and let us choose from among the apparent possibilities the one that speaks more reverently. For this is securely inferred from what is probable: first, that one should accord God the more reverent account, especially in this way, when all suspicions have been cleared away and another adequate and safer supposition is available. Nevertheless, even before the investigation I promise you that every path of inquiry can show him alone—God—to be beyond blame.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς τοῦ θεοῦ τέχνας ἀκριβῶς ἐφευρόντας λέγειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to speak as people who have accurately discovered God’s methods
lexical_decisions.rationale: τέχναι can denote arts, devices, designs, or methods. The participle is represented as describing the capacity in which they would presume to speak; a more strictly temporal rendering would be “to speak after accurately discovering God’s methods.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: [οὗ] τὴν γένεσιν ἡ γραφὴ οὔτε ἀληθὲς [οὔ]τε ψευδὲς εἰπεῖν ἐτόλμησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: about whose origin Scripture did not dare to say either something true or something false
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired negatives portray Scripture as making neither kind of pronouncement about the origin. The wording is preserved rather than simplified to “Scripture says nothing.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν δοκούντων τὸ εὐφημότερον ἑλώμεθα
lexical_decisions.chosen: let us choose from among the apparent possibilities the one that speaks more reverently
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ δοκοῦντα may mean apparent possibilities or proposed opinions. εὐφημότερον is comparative and favors the account that speaks more auspiciously or reverently of God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκ τῶν εἰκότων λαμβάνεται τοῦτο βεβαίως
lexical_decisions.chosen: this is securely inferred from what is probable
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἰκότα are probable considerations rather than certainties. The source’s juxtaposition of probability with secure inference is retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄμεμπτον αὐτὸν μόνον δύναται δεῖξαι τὸν θεόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: can show him alone—God—to be beyond blame
lexical_decisions.rationale: μόνον is taken with αὐτόν, identifying God alone as blameless. It could instead be attached adverbially to δύναται, yielding “can only show God to be blameless.”

source_issues.source_quote: ἐπεὶ ἐκ τῶν εἰκότων λαμβάνεται τοῦτο βεβαίως, ὃ μὲν ὅτι θεῷ τὸ εὐφημότερον δοῦναι πρέπει, ταύτῃ μᾶλλον πασῶν ὑπονοιῶν καθαρθεισῶν καὶ ἄλλης ἱκανῆς καὶ ἀκινδυνοτέρας παρακειμένης ὑποψίας
source_issues.issue: The supplied, image-checked wording is syntactically compressed, especially at ὃ μὲν ὅτι, and no balancing δέ follows μὲν. The translation takes the clause as introducing a first or principal consideration: that the more reverent account should be accorded to God when a sufficient and safer supposition is available. Alternatively, ὃ μὲν may begin an unfinished first reason. No alteration to the selected reading is assumed.

passages.text:
Nevertheless, as you said, if the evil one is something that came into being, then either he came to be as a living creature, or was put forth in substance by God, or was compounded externally; or his choice resulted from the compounding, or it happened to arise without compounding and without God’s counsel. Or he came to be from things that did not exist, or by God from what exists nowhere in any way; or else outside God there was either lifeless or animate matter from which he came to be; or he fashioned himself; or he came into being by God; or he is one of the things that exist in relation to something else; or he always existed. For we cannot say that he does not exist, since we agreed together that he exists.

And Simon said, “You have divided all the paths concerning him well—the main question about him. It is now my part, after scrutinizing the division, to show you that the Creator is liable to blame; but your task is to prove, as you promised, that he is beyond all blame. I wonder whether you will be able to do so. First, if the evil one came into being from God as a living creature, he consequently possesses the same evil as the one who put him forth.”

And Peter said, “Not necessarily. For we see many among human beings who are good yet have fathered bad children, others who are bad yet have had good children, still others who are bad yet produce good offspring, and others who are good yet have become parents of both bad and good children. Thus the first man who was created fathered the unrighteous Cain and the righteous Abel.”

In response Simon said, “You act foolishly by discussing God while using human examples.”

And Peter said, “Then tell us about God without using human examples, while still making it possible for what you say to be understood. But you will not be able to do so.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ γενητός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: if the evil one is something that came into being
lexical_decisions.rationale: γενητός can mean generated, originated, or created. The broader wording avoids deciding in advance which mode of origination the ensuing alternatives support.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐσιωδῶς ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ προβέβληται
lexical_decisions.chosen: was put forth in substance by God
lexical_decisions.rationale: προβάλλω can describe putting forth or emanation, and οὐσιωδῶς indicates that this occurs with respect to substance. The antecedent of αὐτοῦ is understood contextually as God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔξω κέκραται
lexical_decisions.chosen: was compounded externally
lexical_decisions.rationale: κεράννυμι denotes mixing or compounding. ἔξω may mean externally or outside God; the Greek does not explicitly state the reference point here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ ἐκτ[ὸς] ἦν θεοῦ ἢ ὕλη ἄψυχος οὖσα ἢ ἔμψυχος ὅθεν γέγονεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: or else outside God there was either lifeless or animate matter from which he came to be
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering takes ἐκτὸς θεοῦ with the existence of matter and treats ἄψυχος and ἔμψυχος as alternatives describing that matter. It is also possible to divide the sequence as “or he was outside God; or there was lifeless or animate matter from which he came to be.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ τῶν πρὸς τὶ ἐστὶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: or he is one of the things that exist in relation to something else
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ πρός τι is philosophical language for relative or relational entities—things defined through a relation to something else.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Καλῶς πάσας αὐτοῦ τὰς ὁδοὺς διεῖλες, τὸ κεφάλαιον αὐτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: You have divided all the paths concerning him well—the main question about him
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὸ κεφάλαιον may denote a heading, summary, chief point, or principal question. The punctuation leaves its exact attachment compressed, so the translation treats it as an appositional summary of the division.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς αὐτῆς τοῦ προβάλλοντος κακίας τυγχάνει
lexical_decisions.chosen: he consequently possesses the same evil as the one who put him forth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject remains the evil one, while τοῦ προβάλλοντος identifies the producer whose evil Simon infers from the offspring’s nature.

passages.text: For instance, what were you saying at the outset? That if the evil one came into being from God, being of the same substance as God, then God too is evil. But when I showed from the very example you yourself supplied that bad people come from good people and good people from bad people, you did not accept it, saying that the example was human. Therefore I in turn do not now accept that God has been begotten, because begetting belongs to human beings, not to God. But neither can God be good or evil, just or unjust, nor indeed prudent, a living creature, or anything else that can belong to human beings, for such qualities belong to human beings. And if, when investigating God, we must not ascribe to him the good qualities belonging to human beings, there is nothing left to conceive, say, or investigate except this alone: his purpose, which he himself permitted us to understand, so that, when judged, we may be without excuse concerning the things that, although we knew them, we did not keep.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ ἐκ θεοῦ ὁ πονηρὸς γεγένηται, τῆς αὐτῆς αὐτῷ ὢν οὐσίας, καὶ πονηρός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: if the evil one came into being from God, being of the same substance as God, then God too is evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject of the final ἐστιν is implicit. Taking it as God avoids the tautology that the evil one is evil and matches Peter’s summary of Simon’s attempt to blame the Creator. A formally possible but contextually weaker rendering is “then he too is evil.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐ[ξ οὗ]περ αὐτὸς ἔδωκας παραδείγματο[ς]
lexical_decisions.chosen: from the very example you yourself supplied
lexical_decisions.rationale: The emphatic οὗπερ and αὐτός attribute the example to Simon, even though Peter developed its comparison in the preceding exchange.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲ τὸ γεγεννῆσθαι θεὸν παραδέχομαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: I in turn do not now accept that God has been begotten
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect passive infinitive presents God as having undergone generation. The surprising assertion is retained as part of Peter’s reductio rather than changed into “God begets.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε μὴν φρόνιμος ἢ ζῷον
lexical_decisions.chosen: nor indeed prudent, a living creature
lexical_decisions.rationale: φρόνιμος means prudent, sensible, or practically wise. ζῷον is rendered broadly as “a living creature,” preserving Peter’s analogy with human predicates.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ τῆς προαιρέσεως αὐτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: his purpose
lexical_decisions.rationale: προαίρεσις can mean choice, intention, purpose, or moral disposition. Here it refers to the divine purpose made knowable for human accountability.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅπως κρινόμενοι ἀναπολόγητοι ὦμεν περὶ ὧν γνόντες οὐκ ἐφυλάξαμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that, when judged, we may be without excuse concerning the things that, although we knew them, we did not keep
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναπολόγητοι means without a defense or excuse, and φυλάσσω here concerns observing or keeping what was known.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
